claim: Across 839 assessments in 317 experiments, the inter-study gap that maximises retention grows as the retention interval grows. Cepeda et al. (2008) located the optimum at about 20% of the test delay for delays of weeks, falling to about 5% for a one-year delay. (Figures already recorded in research-acting-engine.json topic 3; repeated here only for the gap-versus-interval relationship.)
quote: Analyses suggest that inter-study interval (ISI) and retention interval operate jointly to affect final test retention; specifically, the ISI producing maximal retention increased as retention interval increased.
source: Cepeda, N. J., Pashler, H., Vul, E., Wixted, J. T., & Rohrer, D. (2006). Distributed practice in verbal recall tasks: A review and quantitative synthesis. Psychological Bulletin, 132(3), 354-380. With Cepeda, Vul, Rohrer, Wixted & Pashler (2008), Psychological Science, 19(11), 1095-1102.
establishes: For verbal recall (facts, word lists, paired associates), spaced study beats massed study, and the best gap is not fixed: it depends on how long the material must be retained. Too short and too long a gap both cost retention (a ridge, not a monotonic rule).
doesNotEstablish: It does not establish the gap for motor or performance skills, for whole-scene rehearsal, or for meaning-based learning of a role. The 20%/5% figures come from one fact-learning study (trivia facts) and are not a law for other material.
population: Mostly undergraduates and online adults learning verbal material (2006: 184 articles; 2008: over 1350 online participants learning obscure facts).
uncertainty: High confidence for the direction (spacing helps verbal recall) and for the interaction (optimal gap grows with retention interval). Low confidence that the numerical ratio transfers to acting tasks. Abstract read directly for 2006; 2008 figure as recorded in the companion file.
designImplication: Let learning that is spread across days hold up better at a later performance than the same hours crammed into one day, and let the advantage depend on how far away the performance is. Avoid a single fixed 'ideal gap' constant; at most a soft curve with a broad optimum.

claim: Motor-skill meta-analysis: Lee & Genovese (1988) reviewed 47 articles; distributed practice beat massed practice with a weighted mean effect size of .49 (SD .35) on absolute retention, and the advantage was larger at the end of practice than after a retention interval.
quote: distributed practice is beneficial to both the performance and learning of motor skills, although the effect on performance is greater than the effect on learning (summary of the meta-analysis as reported; abstract-level, not checked against full text)
source: Lee, T. D., & Genovese, E. D. (1988). Distribution of practice in motor skill acquisition: Learning and performance effects reconsidered. Research Quarterly for Exercise and Sport, 59(4), 277-287.
establishes: In laboratory motor tasks, massing trials with short rests depresses performance during practice, and also, by a smaller margin, retained learning. Part of the massed-practice penalty is a temporary performance (fatigue-like) effect, not lost learning.
doesNotEstablish: Lee & Genovese later (1989) reported the effect differs for discrete versus continuous tasks; the review does not cover complex artistic skills or multi-day schedules.
population: Laboratory motor tasks, mostly continuous tracking-type tasks, mostly young adults.
uncertainty: Moderate. Old meta-analysis, small literature, task-type dependent. Search-result summary and abstract only.
designImplication: A long uninterrupted drilling session could show a visible in-session performance dip that partly recovers after rest, i.e. separate 'tired right now' from 'learned less'. Keep the learning penalty smaller than the in-session penalty.

claim: Donovan & Radosevich (1999): overall spaced-vs-massed effect d = 0.46, but the effect was attenuated for more complex tasks and was larger in less rigorous studies.
quote: Now you see it, now you don't (title). Distributed practice effects were attenuated in more complex tasks (reported finding).
source: Donovan, J. J., & Radosevich, D. J. (1999). A meta-analytic review of the distribution of practice effect: Now you see it, now you don't. Journal of Applied Psychology, 84(5), 795-805.
establishes: The spacing benefit is real on average but moderated by task complexity and by the length of the inter-trial interval; complex tasks show smaller benefits, and methodological rigor shrinks the effect.
doesNotEstablish: It does not quantify the effect for any performing-arts task; 'complex' was a coded category, not acting.
population: Mixed laboratory and applied tasks (63 studies as commonly reported), mostly adults.
uncertainty: Moderate. Figures from abstract/summary only. The complexity moderation is the most design-relevant and the least precisely quantified finding.
designImplication: If spacing gives a bonus, make it smaller for complex integrated work (whole-scene rehearsal) than for discrete drillable material (lines, an accent's vowel set).

claim: Shea & Morgan (1979): 72 students learned three movement patterns in blocked or random order. Blocked practice gave better performance during acquisition; random practice gave better retention (10 minutes and 10 days) and better transfer to new, more complex variants.
quote: Retention was greater following random acquisition ... transfer was greater for random acquisition groups than for blocked acquisition groups (abstract wording as reported).
source: Shea, J. B., & Morgan, R. L. (1979). Contextual interference effects on the acquisition, retention, and transfer of a motor skill. Journal of Experimental Psychology: Human Learning and Memory, 5(2), 179-187.
establishes: Practice-session performance and durable learning can dissociate: the schedule that looks worse during practice can produce better retention and transfer.
doesNotEstablish: One lab study on a simple arm-movement task; does not show the effect for sport or artistic skills or for beginners in complex skills.
population: 72 college students, laboratory barrier-knockdown arm movement task.
uncertainty: The founding finding is well replicated in labs; generalisation is contested (see Brady 2004 and the 2023-2025 meta-analytic dispute). Abstract only.
designImplication: Allow a 'mixed drill' practice choice that shows lower immediate session gains but slightly better retention/transfer than a 'blocked drill' choice. Make the trade-off modest and conditional (see next entries).

claim: Magill & Hall (1990) reviewed the contextual-interference literature and concluded there is substantial evidence that high-interference practice aids retention and transfer, while proposing that the effect depends on whether the task variations belong to the same or different motor programmes.
quote: there exists substantial evidence that practice under conditions of high contextual interference can facilitate retention and transfer performance (abstract summary as reported).
source: Magill, R. A., & Hall, K. G. (1990). A review of the contextual interference effect in motor skill acquisition. Human Movement Science, 9(3-5), 241-289.
establishes: A narrative review that the effect is robust in laboratory work and is moderated by how different the practised variations are.
doesNotEstablish: Not a meta-analysis; gives no pooled effect size; field and sport evidence was thinner and more mixed.
population: Reviewed laboratory and some field motor-learning studies.
uncertainty: Moderate; narrative review. Abstract only.
designImplication: Mixing helps most when the mixed items are genuinely different skills or variants (e.g. rotating several accents or several monologues), not trivial variations of one.

claim: Brady (2004) meta-analysis: 139 effect sizes from 61 studies; mean contextual-interference effect .38; basic (lab) research .57 vs applied research .19; adults .50 vs younger learners .10; mean statistical power .43.
quote: average overall effect size of .38 ... basic research (.57) was significantly different from applied research (.19) ... adults (.50) and those for younger learners (.10) (abstract figures as reported).
source: Brady, F. (2004). Contextual interference: A meta-analytic study. Perceptual and Motor Skills, 99(1), 116-126.
establishes: The random-over-blocked benefit is small-to-moderate on average and markedly smaller in applied (real-skill) settings than in laboratory tasks; many studies are underpowered.
doesNotEstablish: Does not establish the benefit for any specific real-world skill, and the applied estimate (.19) is small and uncertain.
population: 61 motor-learning studies, laboratory and applied, children and adults.
uncertainty: Moderate. Later meta-analyses disagree sharply: Ammar et al. (2023/2024) called the sport-practice benefit a 'myth' for gross/sport skills, while Czyz et al. (2024, Scientific Reports) reported that high interference improves retention; each side has published critiques of the other. Abstract only.
designImplication: If a mixed-practice benefit exists in SLATE it should be small, and smaller for real-skill (technique) learning than a lab-style model would suggest. A design that made interleaving a dominant strategy would overclaim.

claim: Recent meta-analyses conflict. Ammar et al. (2023, Educational Research Review; 2024, Educational Psychology Review 36:57) concluded that 'neither the CI effects nor the associated hypotheses can be generalized to gross/sport motor skills', with near-negligible benefits in applied settings. Czyz et al. (2024, Scientific Reports 14:15974) concluded high contextual interference improves retention, with larger effects in adults and older adults than in children.
quote: neither the CI effects nor the associated hypotheses can be generalized to gross/sport motor skills (Ammar et al. 2024, abstract as reported).
source: Ammar, A., et al. (2024). The effects of contextual interference learning on the acquisition and relatively permanent gains in skilled performance: A critical systematic review with multilevel meta-analysis. Educational Psychology Review, 36, 57. Czyz, S. H., Wojcik, A. M., Solarska, P., & Kiper, P. (2024). High contextual interference improves retention in motor learning: systematic review and meta-analysis. Scientific Reports, 14, 15974.
establishes: That the size and generality of the contextual-interference effect outside the laboratory is currently disputed among meta-analysts.
doesNotEstablish: Neither side establishes an effect size for artistic or acting skills.
population: Motor-learning studies; age is a repeated moderator (children show small or no effect).
uncertainty: High disagreement. Both read at abstract/summary level only; full texts paywalled.
designImplication: Treat interleaving as a mild, uncertain modifier. If students are young or novice, the benefit should be smaller still.

claim: Guadagnoli & Lee (2004) propose that learning depends on the information a practice condition generates, which depends on the interaction of the learner's skill level and the task's difficulty. Optimal challenge for learning occurs at lower functional difficulty for less skilled performers and higher for more skilled ones; the condition that maximises learning is not the one that maximises practice performance.
quote: The authors describe the effects of practice conditions in motor learning (e.g., contextual interference, knowledge of results) within the constraints of 2 experimental variables: skill level and task difficulty.
source: Guadagnoli, M. A., & Lee, T. D. (2004). Challenge point: A framework for conceptualizing the effects of various practice conditions in motor learning. Journal of Motor Behavior, 36(2), 212-224.
establishes: A theoretical framework that reconciles contextual-interference and feedback findings: too easy and too hard both yield less learning, and the optimum shifts upward with skill.
doesNotEstablish: It is a conceptual framework, not an empirical estimate. It does not give a numeric 'optimal difficulty' ratio, and a 2025 scoping review (Journal of Motor Behavior) found it widely applied but rarely tested as a whole.
population: Framework built on motor-learning laboratory literature.
uncertainty: Plausible and influential; weakly tested as a quantitative model. Abstract only.
designImplication: Make growth from a piece of material depend on the gap between the student's current level and the material's demand: little growth from material far below level, poor growth (and more failure) from material far above, best in a band just above. Keep the band wide and avoid publishing a precise ratio as 'science'.

claim: Salmoni, Schmidt & Walter (1984) reviewed knowledge-of-results (KR) research and proposed the guidance hypothesis: feedback after every trial guides performance while present but can create dependence, so that conditions best for practice performance are not best for retention without feedback. Winstein & Schmidt (1990) reported that reduced relative frequency of KR (e.g. 50%) produced better delayed retention than 100% KR.
quote: Reduced frequency of knowledge of results enhances motor skill learning (Winstein & Schmidt 1990, title).
source: Salmoni, A. W., Schmidt, R. A., & Walter, C. B. (1984). Knowledge of results and motor learning: A review and critical reappraisal. Psychological Bulletin, 95(3), 355-386. Winstein, C. J., & Schmidt, R. A. (1990). Journal of Experimental Psychology: Learning, Memory, and Cognition, 16(4), 677-691.
establishes: A historically influential hypothesis and supporting lab experiments that constant feedback can help in-session performance more than durable learning.
doesNotEstablish: That reduced feedback reliably improves learning in general: see McKay et al. (2022) next entry.
population: Laboratory motor tasks (timing/positioning), young adults.
uncertainty: Contested; the effect did not survive meta-analysis. Abstracts and summaries only.
designImplication: Do not make 'less teacher feedback = more learning' a rule. At most, distinguish a coach-dependent in-class bump from what the student can do alone at performance.

claim: McKay et al. (2022) meta-analysed 61 articles on reduced relative feedback frequency and found no significant advantage of reduced frequency for acquisition, retention or delayed retention; the literature was heterogeneous and underpowered.
quote: no significant advantage for reduced relative feedback frequency in acquisition, retention, or delayed retention (summary as reported).
source: McKay, B., Hussien, J., Vinh, M.-A., Mir-Orefice, A., Brooks, H., & Ste-Marie, D. M. (2022). Meta-analysis of the reduced relative feedback frequency effect on motor learning and performance. Psychology of Sport and Exercise, 61, 102165.
establishes: The classic 'reduced feedback frequency helps learning' effect is not reliably supported by the pooled evidence.
doesNotEstablish: Does not show feedback is useless or that frequent feedback is harmful; only that the frequency manipulation shows no reliable learning advantage.
population: Motor-learning experiments, mostly laboratory, mixed ages.
uncertainty: Moderate-high confidence in the null; heterogeneity unexplained. Abstract/summary only.
designImplication: Feedback frequency should not be a tuning knob with a claimed optimum. Feedback can matter by content (what it points at), not by a magic rate.

claim: Kluger & DeNisi (1996): across 607 effect sizes (23,663 observations), feedback interventions raised performance on average (d = .41), but over one third of them lowered performance. Their Feedback Intervention Theory holds that feedback becomes less effective as it draws attention away from the task and toward the self.
quote: feedback interventions ... improved performance on average (d = .41) but that over one-third of the FIs decreased performance (abstract wording as widely reported).
source: Kluger, A. N., & DeNisi, A. (1996). The effects of feedback interventions on performance: A historical review, a meta-analysis, and a preliminary feedback intervention theory. Psychological Bulletin, 119(2), 254-284.
establishes: Feedback is not uniformly positive; task-focused feedback tends to help and self-focused (praise/criticism of the person) feedback tends to help less or hurt.
doesNotEstablish: Effects in arts training specifically; the sample is mostly workplace and lab tasks.
population: Mixed laboratory and field studies, mostly adults.
uncertainty: High confidence in heterogeneity; moderate in the attentional explanation. Summary only.
designImplication: Teacher notes could vary in focus: a note about the task ('you rushed the turn') helps more than a note about the person ('you're not a natural'). Allow some notes to backfire, especially for anxious students.

claim: Goodman, Wood & Hendrickx (2004): more specific feedback improved initial practice performance but discouraged exploration and undermined the learning needed for later independent performance.
quote: increasing the specificity of feedback is beneficial for initial performance but discourages exploration and undermines the learning needed for later, more independent performance (abstract as reported).
source: Goodman, J. S., Wood, R. E., & Hendrickx, M. (2004). Feedback specificity, exploration, and learning. Journal of Applied Psychology, 89(2), 248-262.
establishes: A specificity trade-off in a complex decision task: specific feedback = better now, less exploration, weaker transfer to unaided performance. A companion paper (Goodman, Wood & Hendrickx 2004, JAP 89(5)) found the effect depends on what is to be learned.
doesNotEstablish: Does not test motor or artistic skills; not a general law.
population: University students on a computer-simulated management task.
uncertainty: Moderate; single-lab programme. Abstract only.
designImplication: A director giving line readings or exact blocking could raise this performance while lowering the student's own exploratory growth; open notes could grow more independence. Keep the effect small.

claim: Barnett & Ceci (2002) argued a century of transfer research made little progress because studies differ along unstated dimensions; they proposed a taxonomy of content (what transfers) and context (knowledge domain, physical, temporal, functional, social context and modality), with transfer less likely the farther the contexts are apart.
quote: When and where do we apply what we learn? (title) The taxonomy situates each study along nine dimensions (summary as reported).
source: Barnett, S. M., & Ceci, S. J. (2002). When and where do we apply what we learn? A taxonomy for far transfer. Psychological Bulletin, 128(4), 612-637.
establishes: A vocabulary for 'near' vs 'far' transfer and the claim that transfer probability falls with dissimilarity on multiple dimensions.
doesNotEstablish: Gives no transfer rates.
population: Conceptual review.
uncertainty: Framework; not an effect estimate. Summary only.
designImplication: Technique-to-technique transfer should depend on similarity: e.g. stage combat to dance (both choreographed physical) nearer than stage combat to verse. Model a similarity matrix, not a global transfer bonus.

claim: Sala & Gobet (2017) report three meta-analyses (chess instruction, music instruction, working-memory training) and conclude that far transfer to general cognitive or academic skills rarely occurs; effects are small and shrink in better-controlled studies.
quote: Does far transfer exist? Negative evidence from chess, music, and working memory training (title).
source: Sala, G., & Gobet, F. (2017). Does far transfer exist? Negative evidence from chess, music, and working memory training. Current Directions in Psychological Science, 26(6), 515-520.
establishes: Training a specialised skill does not reliably raise distant general abilities.
doesNotEstablish: Says nothing about near transfer within a domain, and does not test acting. Lehman, Lempert & Nisbett (1988) is a counterpoint: graduate psychology and medicine training produced large gains in statistical/methodological reasoning, chemistry training none, suggesting transfer when a field teaches general rule systems.
population: Mostly children (chess, music) and adults (working-memory training).
uncertainty: Contested by some authors but well supported. The PDF could not be text-extracted here; claims from abstract/summaries.
designImplication: Training one technique should not raise unrelated abilities by much. Transfer, where present, should be to closely related techniques or to the general abilities the technique actually exercises.

claim: Noice & Noice found that 'active experiencing' (processing a script for meaning and intention, as actors do) gave non-actors better verbatim retention than intentional memorisation, and that reading aloud while moving to a director's blocking improved retention over verbal-only processing.
quote: participants who processed a script by reading the text aloud while simultaneously moving in accordance with a director's instructions retained more material than did those who used verbal communication only or controls who deliberately memorized the same material (Noice & Noice, Memory & Cognition, 'Learning dialogue with and without movement', abstract as reported).
source: Noice, H., & Noice, T. (2001). Learning dialogue with and without movement. Memory & Cognition, 29(6), 820-827. Noice, H., & Noice, T. (2006). Current Directions in Psychological Science, 15(1), 14-18.
establishes: An actor's meaning-and-action approach to text is a learnable strategy that improves memory for lines even in novices, i.e. near transfer of a learning strategy.
doesNotEstablish: That acting training transfers to general cognition (the older-adult studies are small) or improves performance quality.
population: Undergraduate non-actors with brief coaching; professional actors in related studies.
uncertainty: Moderate; one lab's programme, modest samples. Abstract only. See research-acting-engine.json topic 3 for retention figures.
designImplication: Learning lines with blocking or by working out intentions could memorise faster/stickier than rote repetition. Memory ability can make this a cheaper action rather than a separate system.

claim: Felsman, Gunawardena & Seifert (2020): in two experiments (n = 74, n = 131), 20 minutes of improv exercises increased divergent thinking, uncertainty tolerance and positive affect relative to a matched social control.
quote: after engaging in 20 minutes of improv exercises or a matched control condition including social interactions (design as reported in abstract).
source: Felsman, P., Gunawardena, S., & Seifert, C. M. (2020). Improv experience promotes divergent thinking, uncertainty tolerance, and affective well-being. Thinking Skills and Creativity, 35, 100632.
establishes: Short-term state changes after a single brief improv session in non-actors.
doesNotEstablish: Durable trait change, transfer to scripted acting, or any effect in trained actors. Short-term outcomes measured immediately after.
population: University students / adults, not actors.
uncertainty: Low-moderate; small samples, immediate outcomes. Abstract only. Wider literature on improv and creativity/self-concept (e.g. DeBettignies & Goldstein 2020, children) is small and methodologically uneven.
designImplication: An improv class could give a short-lived boost to adaptability or composure state (e.g. for the next rehearsal) rather than large permanent ability gains.

claim: Macnamara, Moreau & Hambrick (2016): in sports, deliberate practice explained 18% of performance variance overall and only 1% among elite performers. (Macnamara et al. 2014 cross-domain figures, e.g. 21% music, are in research-acting-engine.json topic 2.)
quote: deliberate practice accounted for 18% of the variance in sports performance ... only 1% of the variance in performance among elite-level performers (figures as reported).
source: Macnamara, B. N., Moreau, D., & Hambrick, D. Z. (2016). The relationship between deliberate practice and performance in sports: A meta-analysis. Perspectives on Psychological Science, 11(3), 333-350.
establishes: Accumulated practice correlates with performance but leaves most variance unexplained, and differences in practice explain almost nothing among people who all practise a lot.
doesNotEstablish: That practice does not matter, or that the rest is 'talent': unexplained variance includes measurement error, starting age, quality of instruction, and other factors. Ericsson (2016) disputed the definition of deliberate practice used.
population: Athletes across skill levels; retrospective practice estimates.
uncertainty: Moderate; correlational, retrospective self-report, definitional dispute. Summary only.
designImplication: Hours of practice should be a major but not sole driver; let starting aptitude, teaching quality, health and luck matter. Among strong students, extra hours should differentiate little.

claim: Michael Caine teaches that film performance must be scaled down from stage: the microphone and camera pick up everything, so projection and stage-size gesture read as false; in close-up 'less is more' in voice and action.
quote: In movies, the microphone can always hear you, no matter how softly you speak, no matter where the scene is taking place. (Also: in terms of voice and action, less is more; theatre-trained performance can look 'suddenly exaggerated and false' on film.)
source: Caine, M. (1990). Acting in Film: An Actor's Take on Movie Making. Applause. Quotations via Acting Magazine (2022) secondary report.
establishes: An authoritative practitioner's pedagogy that screen scale differs from stage scale and that excess projection reads as false on camera.
doesNotEstablish: Any measured threshold of 'too big'. Not empirical; one practitioner's craft account (widely shared in screen-acting pedagogy).
population: Professional film acting; practitioner testimony.
uncertainty: Quotations come from a secondary source, not checked against the book page. Treat the wording as approximate except the microphone sentence.
designImplication: A 'performance scale' choice could interact with medium: large projection helps a big stage, costs on camera close-up. Scale mismatch rather than a fixed penalty.

claim: Patrick Tucker's screen-acting pedagogy teaches matching the size of the performance to the size of the shot: close-ups need small, contained expression; wide shots allow larger physicality; vocal level is adjusted to the frame.
quote: No verbatim Tucker quotation was verified in this pass. Secondary summary: large movements which might work in a medium or wide shot can overwhelm a close-up (Acting Coach Scotland paraphrase of Tucker).
source: Tucker, P. (1994; 3rd ed. 2003/2014). Secrets of Screen Acting. Routledge.
establishes: Practitioner pedagogy that performance scale should be calibrated to shot size, not just to medium.
doesNotEstablish: Empirical evidence about audience perception of scale.
population: Screen actors trained by Tucker (RADA, BBC); practitioner text.
uncertainty: Paraphrase only; book is borrow-only on Internet Archive and was not read. Barton (1984, p.145) independently notes the stage counterpart: a big auditorium pushes actors to enlarge voice and emotion and a speech played lightly in rehearsal 'can become forced'.
designImplication: Treat scale as relative to venue/shot: a calibration skill (screen technique) reduces the mismatch penalty. Stage venue size could also push scale up.

claim: John Barton (RSC) teaches that the verse carries direction: shared lines mean pick up the cue at once; short lines indicate a pause; end-stopped lines are the norm; naturalistic habit adds too many pauses; but whether to pause at a caesura is determined by the character's intention, and one tone/one tempo is a trap.
quote: The second speaker is meant to pick up the cue at once, as surely as if Shakespeare had written in the stage-direction, 'don't pause here'. (p.32) ... It's no good if the richness and complexity of the verse leads one to think slowly and laboriously. Our naturalistic bias makes us use a large number of pauses, both at the end of the line and within it. (p.32) ... It's a great trap with Shakespeare's text if you get on to one note, one tone and one tempo. (p.51)
source: Barton, J. (1984). Playing Shakespeare. Methuen. Quotations via SHAKSPER reference notes with page numbers.
establishes: A canonical RSC pedagogy in which verse form constrains pace and pausing (fewer, placed pauses; pick-up on shared lines) while leaving interpretive choice inside the form.
doesNotEstablish: That there is one correct reading, or any measured audience effect. Practitioner pedagogy.
population: RSC actors (workshop series, 1982 TV; book 1984).
uncertainty: Page-numbered secondary notes, read directly; not checked against the book itself.
designImplication: Verse material can constrain pace choices: excessive pausing or slow, laboured delivery could be penalised in verse more than in naturalistic prose, and monotone tempo penalised; within-line pauses allowed when motivated.

claim: Peter Hall held that form comes before feeling: the actor must keep the verse form and the tension between form and emotion moves the audience; secondary summaries of his book add rules such as observing the line ending, breathing at line ends, and not pausing mid-line if the sense continues.
quote: Real, credible theatre has to put form before feeling ... it's the tension between the form and the feeling which actually excites the audience. (Web of Stories interview) Attributed to Shakespeare's Advice to the Players: 'Never pause in the middle of a line if the sense continues' (secondary, unverified).
source: Hall, P. (2003). Shakespeare's Advice to the Players. Oberon. Hall, P. interview, Web of Stories, segment 28.
establishes: A directorial school (Hall/Barton RSC) in which verse structure limits pausing and pace choices; Hall's Ophelia example argues strong emotion must be held within the form rather than released over it.
doesNotEstablish: Consensus: other practitioners (e.g. some Method-influenced directors) allow freer pausing. Not empirical.
population: Practitioner pedagogy.
uncertainty: Interview quotation read directly; the 'never pause' rule is from a search summary only. Cicely Berry: no verbatim line-ending quotation was verified this pass; secondary sources say she drew attention to 'the implied pause in the middle of a line' and used 'walking the line' exercises.
designImplication: In verse, emotional depth without verse technique could tip into a form break (lost line, wrong pause) and cost the scene; emotion contained by technique could score highest. A verse technique gates how much emotion can be spent.

claim: Feydeau farce is described as mechanically constructed, with detailed stage directions that leave little flexibility to actors; small departures disturb the balance.
quote: Feydeau's detailed stage directions ... allow little flexibility for directors or actors ... even the slightest change can disrupt the delicate balance. A Flea in Her Ear functions as a 'rigorously, logically constructed machine'.
source: Gale Contextual Encyclopedia of World Literature, 'Feydeau, Georges', via Encyclopedia.com.
establishes: A scholarly-reference characterisation that farce demands precision of timing and blocking (a physical/ensemble precision demand).
doesNotEstablish: Measured evidence that comic timing is material-specific. No empirical study comparing actors' timing across farce vs high comedy was found.
population: Literary-reference description.
uncertainty: Secondary reference, read directly. Bergson's 'mechanical encrusted on the living' (in research-acting-engine.json topic 10) is the theory behind it.
designImplication: Farce could weight physical precision, ensemble timing and stamina; errors of timing could be costlier (one dropped cue breaks the machine).

claim: High comedy (Wilde, Coward) is taught as verbal: Maria Aitken's acting text treats language as character and stresses knowing lines thoroughly to deliver heightened wit naturally.
quote: No verbatim Aitken quotation verified. Secondary summary: to make the witty and heightened language of high comedy more natural to the actor and accessible to the audience, the actor must know his or her lines inside and out; in high comedy the character is the language.
source: Aitken, M. (1996). Style: Acting in High Comedy. Applause.
establishes: A practitioner's position that high comedy depends on verbal dexterity and line security, as opposed to farce's physical precision.
doesNotEstablish: Empirical difference in skill demands; only pedagogy.
population: Practitioner text.
uncertainty: Summary only; book not read.
designImplication: Comedy of manners could weight vocal expression, memory (line security) and verbal comedy technique more than physical comedy. The split between farce and high comedy is a pedagogy-grounded design choice, not a measured fact.

claim: Chekhov insisted The Cherry Orchard was 'not a drama but a comedy, in places even a farce'; Stanislavski staged it as tragedy. The tonal dispute has persisted in production since.
quote: not a drama, but a comedy, in places even a farce (Chekhov to M. P. Lilina, 15 September 1903, as widely quoted).
source: Chekhov, A. Letter to Maria Lilina, 1903; see 'The Cherry Orchard', Wikipedia, and Encyclopedia.com 'The Cherry Orchard'.
establishes: That mixed-tone material is contested and that the same play can be played comic or tragic; the performance choice of tone matters.
doesNotEstablish: That tragicomedy requires a distinct measurable 'transition' skill. No empirical source found.
population: Historical record.
uncertainty: Quote widely reproduced; letter date per secondary sources.
designImplication: Mixed-tone material could reward adaptability (switching register) and penalise playing one register throughout; the 'right' tone could be a director's choice rather than fixed.

claim: Kast & Leukel (2016): expert handball players (n = 19) produced more consistent throwing outcomes than novices (n = 18) and made smaller corrections after visual perturbation.
quote: experts produced higher consistency of motor outcome. They were still susceptible to the sensory feedback informing about motor error, but made smaller adjustments than novices.
source: Kast, V., & Leukel, C. (2016). Motor experts care about consistency and are reluctant to change motor outcome. PLoS One, 11(8), e0161798.
establishes: In one aimed motor task, expertise was associated with lower outcome variability.
doesNotEstablish: Generality across tasks; cross-sectional, so cannot separate training from selection.
population: 37 young adults; experts were amateur/semi-professional handball players with 12+ years.
uncertainty: Small sample, single task. Abstract read directly.
designImplication: Higher skill could narrow the spread of performance outcomes (fewer bad nights) as well as raise the mean.

claim: A 2026 scoping review of 52 studies found intra-individual outcome variability generally decreases with skill, but movement variability is not simply reduced: experts reduce variability in performance-critical parameters while keeping functional variability elsewhere to adapt.
quote: Classical motor learning theory posits that skill acquisition involves reducing variability, yet alternative evidence suggests that variability can be functional and may not uniformly decrease with skill acquisition. ... the quality and structure of variability, rather than its sheer magnitude, are key indicators of motor expertise.
source: Tsunoda, K., Kusafuka, A., Furukawa, H., et al., & Kudo, K. (2026). The relationship between motor variability and skill level: A scoping review. SportRxiv preprint.
establishes: Outcome consistency tends to rise with expertise; process variability can stay or rise where it serves adaptation.
doesNotEstablish: Peer review (preprint); no performing-arts data; no rate.
population: 52 motor-skill studies (sport, music etc.).
uncertainty: Preprint; moderate. Abstract read directly.
designImplication: Model expertise as lower variance in outcome while allowing varied, responsive choices: consistency should not mean identical performances each night.

claim: Lim & Dinges (2010): short-term total sleep deprivation hits simple attention hardest (lapses g = -0.776, 95% CI -0.96 to -0.60) and leaves reasoning accuracy largely spared (g = -0.125, CI -0.27 to 0.02, ns). Doran, Van Dongen & Dinges (2001) found performance variability increases markedly with continued sleep loss (state instability).
quote: Effect sizes ranged from small and nonsignificant (reasoning accuracy: g = -0.125, 95% CI [-0.27, 0.02]) to large (lapses in simple attention: g = -0.776, 95% CI [-0.96, -0.60], p < .001).
source: Lim, J., & Dinges, D. F. (2010). Psychological Bulletin, 136(3), 375-389. Doran, S. M., Van Dongen, H. P. A., & Dinges, D. F. (2001). Sustained attention performance during sleep deprivation: Evidence of state instability. Archives Italiennes de Biologie, 139, 253-267.
establishes: Bounds for condition effects: large effects on vigilance/attention, moderate on working memory, little on reasoning; and that fatigue raises variability (more lapses), not just lowers the mean.
doesNotEstablish: Effects of ordinary tiredness short of 24-48 h total deprivation; effects on artistic performance quality.
population: Healthy adults in laboratory deprivation studies (70 articles, 147 tests).
uncertainty: High for direction and ranking. Note: research-acting-engine.json records lapses as 0.762; the published abstract gives -0.776 for lapses. One of the two figures should be reconciled against the full text.
designImplication: Fatigue should affect focus/concentration and memory-like demands more than interpretive judgement, and should widen the spread of outcomes (more chance of a lapse, a dropped line) rather than only shift the average. Bound the penalty to well under a full standard-deviation-sized hit except at extreme deprivation.

claim: Meisner's two stated basic principles locate the actor's behaviour in response to the partner.
quote: There are two basic principles involved here ... 'Don't do anything unless something happens to make you do it.' That's one of them. The second is: 'What you do doesn't depend on you; it depends on the other fellow.' ... If you repeat what you get from him, you won't be at a loss for something to say.
source: Meisner, S., & Longwell, D. (1987). Sanford Meisner on Acting. Vintage. Internet Archive text.
establishes: The canonical pedagogy that listening and responding to the partner, not pre-planned delivery, is the core of truthful behaviour.
doesNotEstablish: Measured effects of Meisner training on listening or audience judgement.
population: Practitioner pedagogy (Neighborhood Playhouse classes).
uncertainty: Quotes read from an OCR text via a summarising fetch; wording consistent with widely quoted versions.
designImplication: A scene's quality could depend partly on the partner's output (a responsive actor plays better opposite a giving partner), and listening could convert a partner's strength into one's own performance.

claim: Noy, Dekel & Alon (2011) used the theatre mirror game to show that experienced improvisers (actors and musicians) can jointly create novel complex motion with no designated leader, synchronised to under 40 ms, in 'co-confident' periods.
quote: players can jointly create novel complex motion without a designated leader, synchronized to less than 40 ms (abstract as reported).
source: Noy, L., Dekel, E., & Alon, U. (2011). The mirror game as a paradigm for studying the dynamics of two people improvising motion together. PNAS, 108(52), 20947-20952.
establishes: Mutual, leaderless coordination is measurable and achievable at high precision by expert improvisers; joint improvisation is a property of the pair.
doesNotEstablish: That listening is a trainable single trait, or that it predicts scene quality; small expert sample.
population: Expert improvisers (actors and jazz musicians), small sample; later work (e.g. 2015 Human Movement Science) studied acquisition.
uncertainty: Moderate; PNAS full text returned 403; abstract-level.
designImplication: Ensemble or partner work could have a pair-level quality that exceeds the average of the two individuals when both are responsive (listening/adaptability), rather than being a sum of solo scores.

claim: Searches this pass found no empirical study that (a) measures comic timing as material-specific (farce vs high comedy), (b) measures transfer between acting techniques, (c) measures audience perception of stage-scale performance on camera, or (d) measures growth rates of acting abilities under different practice schedules.
source: Web searches, 2026-10-10.
establishes: That the acting-specific mechanics listed are grounded in practitioner pedagogy, not measurement.
doesNotEstablish: That such studies do not exist; only that they were not found.
population: n/a
uncertainty: Search-limited.
designImplication: Present these mechanics as craft conventions, keep their magnitudes modest and tunable, and avoid in-game text that cites 'research' for numbers.
